governanceStructure: Wootlab Foundation operates under a Board of Trustees, which provides the highest level of governance and strategic oversight. The Board ensures that the Foundation remains aligned with its mission, values, legal responsibilities, and long-term objectives. The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) provides executive leadership and is accountable to the Board of Trustees for the overall management and performance of the Foundation. The CEO translates the Board’s strategic direction into organisational priorities and ensures effective stewardship of resources. The Team Lead supports the CEO by coordinating day-to-day organisational activities and ensuring that the Foundation’s core functions Programmes, Communications & Media, Resource Mobilisation, Administration, and Operations work together effectively toward shared organisational goals. In summary: Board of Trustees → Strategic Governance & Oversight CEO → Executive Leadership & Accountability Team Lead → Coordination & Implementation Oversight Core Functions → Delivery of Organisational Objectives
programmeDeliveryTrackRecord: Wootlab Foundation has a strong track record of designing and implementing large-scale digital skills, entrepreneurship, education, and capacity-building programmes across Nigeria and beyond. Its delivery experience spans partnerships with government institutions, Microsoft, multinational organisations, financial institutions, development partners, and private-sector organisations, with programmes reaching beneficiaries across multiple states and underserved communities. Key delivery experience includes: Large-scale digital skills delivery: Over 120,000 Nigerian youths trained through the Federal Government–Microsoft Digital Skills Nigeria initiative, alongside programmes reaching tens of thousands of additional beneficiaries across states. Digital community implementation: Operationalisation of 50 Digital Community Centres across 17 states, managing 100 facilitators and training over 21,393 beneficiaries between August and May. Youth and employability programmes: More than 26,000 beneficiaries trained in Anambra across digital skills, entrepreneurship and career pathways, with selected beneficiaries receiving laptops and internship opportunities. Public-sector capacity building: Delivery of digital upskilling programmes for civil servants, including 210 OHCSF participants in 2024 and 500 civil servants in 2025 across key federal institutions. Teacher development: Implementation of the Seplat Teachers Empowerment Programme, including 650 teachers trained in 2025 and a cumulative 1,984 teachers empowered since inception. Women and girls in technology: Programmes including RevUp Women and Girls in ICT initiatives, reaching women entrepreneurs and over 335 female secondary-school students, respectively. Digital learning infrastructure: Extensive deployment of the Microsoft Community Training (MCT) Platform, with over 300,000 registered learners through 57 partner organisations and programmes since 2022. Enterprise development: Delivery of entrepreneurship programmes, including support to 375 business owners in Kwara, with 170 businesses qualifying for loan support and over ₦102 million disbursed to eligible businesses. Inclusive digital skills: Training of over 10,800 young people across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe, with deliberate inclusion of women and Persons with Disabilities. Overall, this track record demonstrates Wootlab Foundation’s capacity to manage multi-stakeholder programmes, deliver at scale, leverage digital learning platforms, coordinate distributed implementation teams, and translate training investments into measurable participation, certification, employability and enterprise outcomes.

inclusionAccessibilityCapacity: Gender Equality, Social Inclusion and Equity (GESI) will be integrated throughout the programme lifecycle, from mobilisation and beneficiary selection to training, assessment, employment and ongoing monitoring. The programme will maintain a 50/50 gender balance and target at least 5% participation from young people who are Not in Employment, Education or Training (NEET), while deliberately creating opportunities for Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) and other marginalised and underserved groups. To promote gender parity, participation will be actively monitored from the application stage through enrolment, attendance, completion, certification and placement, with all relevant data disaggregated by gender. Targeted mobilisation strategies will be used to increase female participation, including engagement with women’s groups, faith-based organisations, female ambassadors, recruiters and trainers. Female application and conversion rates will also be monitored by state and mobilisation channel to identify and address gaps in participation. The programme will also prioritise operational accessibility and safe participation for all beneficiaries. Training venues will be selected to promote safety and accessibility, while flexible schedules will be considered to accommodate participants with different needs. Where approved and feasible, additional support such as childcare or transport assistance may be provided to reduce barriers to participation. Attendance, retention and withdrawal patterns will be monitored to identify challenges that may disproportionately affect vulnerable participants. For Persons with Disabilities, the programme will actively create pathways for participation through targeted mobilisation and partnerships with organisations such as the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD), the Joint National Association of Persons with Disabilities (JONAPWD) and other disability-focused organisations. Accessibility assessments will inform programme delivery, while participation, reasonable accommodation, completion and placement outcomes for PWDs will be specifically tracked. The programme will further adopt targeted approaches to reach NEETs and other vulnerable groups, including young people in underserved communities and internally displaced persons (IDPs). Community-based partners, social-welfare actors and other relevant stakeholders will support outreach to these groups. Where required, participants will receive reasonable accommodation, including assistive technologies, adapted learning materials and individual support plans, based on identified needs. GESI considerations will extend beyond training into employment and placement. The programme will engage employers that demonstrate disability-inclusive practices and provide workplace-readiness and placement support to participants. Employer inclusion practices and PWD placement outcomes will be monitored to ensure that inclusion is reflected not only in programme participation but also in access to employment opportunities. Overall accountability for GESI implementation will be supported through GESI Specialist oversight, weekly monitoring and quarterly inclusion reporting. Participation and outcome data will be reviewed regularly to identify disparities, track progress against inclusion targets and implement corrective actions where necessary. This approach will ensure that GESI is treated as a core programme delivery principle rather than a standalone activity.
existingInstitutionalRelationships: Wootlab Foundation has established relationships and experience working with tertiary institutions, including institutions within the North Central region. Our existing engagements include the University of Abuja and Nile University, providing a strong foundation for collaboration, institutional mobilisation and programme implementation. Beyond North Central, Wootlab has also worked with institutions including Igbinedion University and the University of Uyo, giving our team practical experience in navigating institutional structures, engaging university leadership and working with faculty, student-facing departments and other relevant stakeholders. For the iDICE Programme, we are already engaging with prospective host institutions to build institutional buy-in, understand their existing entrepreneurship and enterprise support structures, and establish clear focal points for programme coordination. These relationships will support faster mobilisation, beneficiary identification and referral, access to relevant institutional facilities and networks, and effective coordination throughout implementation. Our approach is therefore built on existing institutional relationships, early engagement and strong stakeholder ownership, enabling Wootlab to integrate enterprise support into existing institutional structures while ensuring that participating beneficiaries receive consistent and practical support.
institutionalCoordinationPlan: Wootlab Foundation will work closely with existing institutional structures to ensure that enterprise support is embedded within, rather than operating separately from, the institutions. We are already engaging participating institutions to secure leadership buy-in, establish clear coordination mechanisms and align implementation with existing entrepreneurship, career development and student support structures. We will work with entrepreneurship and innovation centres, career services units, student affairs departments, alumni networks and relevant faculties to support outreach, beneficiary identification, referrals, enterprise development activities and post-programme engagement. Where institutions have entrepreneurship or innovation hubs, these will serve as key entry points for enterprise support, mentoring and engagement with beneficiaries. Wootlab has extensive experience working with universities and tertiary institutions, including the University of Abuja and Nile University in the North Central region, as well as Igbinedion University and the University of Uyo in other regions. These engagements have strengthened our understanding of institutional processes and our ability to work collaboratively with university leadership, staff, faculty and student-facing structures.
staffFacultyEngagementPlan: Wootlab will engage designated institutional staff and faculty as key implementation partners throughout the programme. During mobilisation, we will work with relevant focal persons to communicate programme objectives, identify eligible beneficiaries and facilitate access to existing student, alumni and entrepreneurship networks. We will establish clear institutional focal points who will coordinate with the Wootlab implementation team and support communication between the programme and relevant university structures. Staff and faculty will also be oriented on the programme's objectives, eligibility requirements, referral process and available enterprise support so they can effectively identify and recommend suitable beneficiaries. Faculty members, entrepreneurship centre personnel and career services staff will be encouraged to identify promising student and graduate entrepreneurs within their networks and connect them to relevant programme opportunities. Where appropriate, institutional staff may also participate in enterprise-focused sessions, mentoring, networking and other activities based on their expertise. Our previous engagements with institutions such as the University of Abuja, Nile University, Igbinedion University and University of Uyo provide a strong foundation for effective institutional collaboration.
beneficiaryReferralPlan: Beneficiaries will be identified through a combination of institution-led mobilisation, targeted outreach and structured application and screening processes. Wootlab will work with institutional focal persons, entrepreneurship centres, career services, faculties, student affairs units and alumni networks to reach eligible students, graduates and entrepreneurs. Institutions will be provided with clear eligibility and referral criteria to enable staff and faculty to identify potential beneficiaries, particularly individuals with viable business ideas, existing enterprises or clear entrepreneurial potential who can benefit from the programme's support. Wootlab will complement institutional referrals with direct mobilisation through its established digital and community networks, ensuring that outreach extends beyond beneficiaries already connected to entrepreneurship centres. All applicants will undergo a transparent screening process against agreed programme criteria, with attention to inclusion and equitable participation. Beneficiary data will be captured through a structured registration and verification process, allowing Wootlab to track participation, support provided, enterprise progress and outcomes throughout the programme. This approach will combine the reach and institutional knowledge of partner institutions with Wootlab's experience in large-scale beneficiary mobilisation and programme delivery.
monitoringReportingSystems: Wootlab Foundation uses structured digital systems for beneficiary registration, attendance, participation, performance tracking and post-programme monitoring. Our programme delivery is supported by digital dashboards and data collection tools that enable real-time tracking of beneficiary engagement and programme outputs across multiple locations. We use standardised data collection and verification processes to ensure that beneficiary information is captured accurately and can be disaggregated by relevant indicators such as gender, location, institution and programme participation. Programme teams regularly review data to identify gaps, monitor performance against targets and inform implementation decisions. Our experience managing large-scale programmes has strengthened our capacity for data quality assurance, reporting and evidence-based programme management. We provide periodic implementation and outcome reports to partners and stakeholders, supported by beneficiary-level data, attendance records, activity reports and documented results. For iDICE, we will maintain a centralised monitoring framework covering beneficiary onboarding, enterprise support activities, mentorship, milestones, referrals and post-programme outcomes, with clear reporting responsibilities and data protection protocols.
sustainabilityPlan: Wootlab Foundation's sustainability approach combines strategic partnerships, programme diversification and the ability to mobilise resources from development partners, private-sector organisations and institutional funders. We do not intend for enterprise support activities to depend solely on a single funding source. Wootlab will leverage its established relationships with development organisations, government institutions, technology partners, universities and private-sector stakeholders to identify opportunities for continued enterprise development support. We will also pursue competitive grants, corporate social responsibility partnerships and co-funded programmes aligned with youth employment, entrepreneurship, digital skills and inclusive economic development. In addition, Wootlab's wider organisational ecosystem, including its technical and talent development capabilities, provides opportunities to connect trained entrepreneurs and skilled beneficiaries to private-sector opportunities. Lessons, tools and institutional relationships developed through the programme will be integrated into future enterprise and employability initiatives, creating a foundation for continued support beyond the iDICE programme. Our sustainability model therefore focuses on diversifying funding, strengthening partnerships and building institutional capacity, rather than relying on one programme or revenue stream.
employmentPathway: Wootlab will design the programme around a clear progression from enterprise support to income generation, employment and business growth. Beneficiaries will first be assessed to understand their skills, business stage and career or enterprise goals. Based on this assessment, they will receive targeted capacity development, mentorship and practical support relevant to their pathway. For employment-oriented beneficiaries, Wootlab will facilitate exposure to industry, career guidance, skills development and referrals to relevant employment opportunities. Beneficiaries demonstrating the required competencies will be connected to employers and talent networks, while those pursuing entrepreneurship will receive enterprise-focused mentoring and support to strengthen their business models, customer acquisition and readiness for growth. Wootlab will track key transition points, including completion, employment or self-employment, enterprise activity, referrals and income-generating outcomes. This creates a practical pathway of identification → assessment → skills/enterprise support → industry exposure → referral → employment or enterprise growth → post-programme tracking. Our experience in digital skills, employability and talent development, alongside the capabilities of Wootlab Innovations, will enable us to strengthen the transition between programme participation and real economic opportunities.

governanceStructure: Engee Ecodesigns Limited operates with a clear management and governance structure that supports accountability, effective decision-making and responsible programme delivery. The Founder and CEO provides overall strategic leadership, business oversight and stakeholder engagement, and is responsible for ensuring that organisational goals and programme commitments are achieved. The operations and programme functions support day-to-day implementation, including training coordination, beneficiary engagement, production activities, partnerships and reporting. For programmes and enterprise-support activities, responsibilities are assigned to designated team members based on their expertise, with clear supervision and defined deliverables. Financial and administrative activities are managed through documented processes, including budgeting, record keeping, expenditure tracking and reporting. The organisation also works with consultants, trainers and technical personnel where specialised expertise is required. Key decisions are reviewed by management to ensure alignment with organisational objectives, safeguarding requirements, gender inclusion, environmental and social considerations, and applicable laws and policies. Engee maintains accountability to partners and beneficiaries through activity documentation, monitoring of outputs and outcomes, financial records, and periodic reporting. This structure enables the organisation to manage partnerships, deliver training and enterprise-support activities, monitor performance and continuously improve its programmes.
programmeDeliveryTrackRecord: Engee Ecodesigns Limited has practical experience designing and delivering skills development, entrepreneurship and circular-fashion programmes for young people and women, particularly within underserved communities. Since our establishment in 2021, we have trained and reached more than 300 young people and women through hands-on activities focused on upcycling, fashion design, product development, entrepreneurship and sustainable livelihood opportunities. Our approach combines practical learning with real-world production, enabling participants to develop skills that can be applied to income-generating activities and employment. Our programmes have included practical demonstrations, guided production sessions, mentoring and business-oriented learning. Participants are exposed to the full process from identifying and preparing post-consumer textile waste to developing marketable fashion and lifestyle products, while also learning about product development and entrepreneurship. Engee has also implemented activities through partnerships and ecosystem programmes, including engagements supported by organisations such as We For Good Foundation/IHS Sustainable Solutions Africa, Amahoro Coalition, NCIC and YALI. These experiences have strengthened our capacity in programme coordination, participant engagement, partnership management, documentation and reporting. Our delivery model is practical, inclusive and community-oriented. We are experienced in working with young people and displaced and underserved communities and understand the importance of accessible training, mentorship, safeguarding and follow-up support. We intend to build on this experience to deliver structured enterprise support, mentorship and creative skills development under the Wootlab programme.
mentorshipIndustryNetwork: Engee Ecodesigns Limited has developed relationships across the entrepreneurship, sustainability, fashion and youth-development ecosystem through participation in structured programmes, partnerships, training opportunities and industry engagements. Through programmes and networks including the Amahoro Coalition Fellowship, IHS Sustainable Solutions Africa/We For Good Foundation, NCIC and YALI, Engee has gained access to mentors, business development support, peer networks and ecosystem stakeholders. These engagements have provided opportunities for strategic guidance, learning, partnerships and exposure to organisations working across entrepreneurship, sustainability and inclusive economic development. Our industry network also includes relationships within the fashion and creative sector, particularly around sustainable fashion, product development, textile waste management and skills development. We engage with customers, creatives, suppliers, community stakeholders and organisations that provide opportunities for collaboration, market access and programme delivery. Engee is continuing to strengthen its access to investors and financing partners as the business scales. Our focus is on building long-term relationships with impact-oriented funders, sustainability-focused organisations, private-sector partners and other stakeholders interested in circular economy, youth employment and creative enterprise development. These networks provide a foundation for connecting programme beneficiaries to mentors, industry practitioners, potential customers, partners and appropriate financing opportunities while expanding Engee's capacity to deliver enterprise support.
inclusionAccessibilityCapacity: Engee Ecodesigns Limited will build inclusion into participant recruitment, training delivery and follow-up to achieve at least 40% female participation and 5% NEET youth participation. We will set these targets at the recruitment stage and work with youth groups, community organisations, local networks and other relevant stakeholders to reach eligible participants. We will deliberately encourage applications from young women and unemployed or out-of-school youth who may not have access to conventional entrepreneurship programmes. For female participation, we will maintain a safe and respectful learning environment, use accessible communication channels and, where possible, consider training schedules that accommodate caregiving responsibilities. Participation will be monitored by gender throughout recruitment and programme delivery, allowing us to increase targeted outreach if female participation falls below the 40% target. For the NEET target, we will identify participants who are not currently in employment, education or training during registration and maintain a separate participation record. Community-based mobilisation and direct outreach will help us reach young people who are less likely to access formal opportunities. We will regularly review disaggregated participation data against both targets and take corrective action where necessary. Beyond participation, we will provide practical, market-oriented skills, mentorship and enterprise support to help participants progress towards employment, self-employment or further enterprise development.
existingInstitutionalRelationships: Engee Ecodesigns Limited does not currently have a formal partnership with the designated host institution in FCT. However, we have engaged with the wider enterprise-support ecosystem and previously participated in a Wootlab programme, gaining exposure to structured enterprise development and support activities. We have also developed working relationships with organisations, community stakeholders and ecosystem partners through our skills-development, entrepreneurship and sustainability activities. These experiences have strengthened our capacity to engage stakeholders, mobilise participants, coordinate programmes and deliver practical training. If selected, Engee will work closely with the designated host institution to establish an effective working arrangement, clearly define responsibilities and leverage the institution's networks and facilities to deliver the programme successfully.
institutionalCoordinationPlan: Engee will coordinate with the host institution through a designated focal team and a clear implementation sequence. First, we will map the relevant entrepreneurship centre, career services, student affairs and alumni networks and agree on roles, communication channels, referral processes and delivery timelines. Second, these structures will support targeted beneficiary mobilisation. Entrepreneurship centres will help identify participants interested in enterprise development, student affairs will support outreach and engagement, career services will help reach employment-seeking youth, while alumni networks will extend outreach and provide mentorship and industry connections. Third, Engee will deliver practical creative-enterprise training, mentorship and enterprise-support activities in coordination with institutional schedules and existing programmes. Regular coordination meetings will help resolve operational issues and prevent duplication. Fourth, participants will be connected to mentors, industry practitioners, employers, customers and relevant ecosystem opportunities through the institution's networks and Engee's wider partnerships. Finally, we will jointly monitor participation, training completion, enterprise activity and employment outcomes. Regular reviews will be used to identify gaps, improve delivery and ensure progress towards programme targets. This approach will integrate the Centre of Excellence into existing institutional structures while leveraging Engee's practical expertise in creative enterprise, sustainable fashion and entrepreneurship support.
staffFacultyEngagementPlan: Engee will engage institutional staff and faculty through a structured coordination and implementation process to ensure effective programme delivery and strong institutional ownership. First, we will identify key staff and faculty across entrepreneurship, career services, student affairs, relevant academic departments and alumni engagement units, and establish designated focal persons for the programme. An initial briefing will align stakeholders on the programme objectives, beneficiary targets, implementation timeline, roles and reporting requirements. Second, staff and faculty will support participant mobilisation by sharing programme information through institutional communication channels, departments, student networks and relevant staff contacts. Faculty members will also help identify students and young people who may benefit from the creative-enterprise and entrepreneurship opportunities. Third, Engee will work with relevant faculty and staff to align training activities with institutional schedules and existing entrepreneurship or employability initiatives. Where appropriate, faculty members and experienced staff can contribute as guest facilitators, mentors or technical advisers, while Engee provides practical expertise in sustainable fashion, upcycling and creative enterprise. Fourth, we will maintain regular communication through scheduled coordination meetings, progress updates and feedback sessions. Staff and faculty will be able to raise operational issues, recommend improvements and support timely resolution of challenges. Finally, institutional staff and faculty will be involved in monitoring participation, training completion, enterprise activities and post-training outcomes. Their continued involvement will help strengthen referrals, mentorship, industry connections and sustainability beyond the programme period. This approach will ensure that the Centre is integrated into the institution’s existing structures rather than operating as a standalone project.
beneficiaryReferralPlan: Beneficiaries will be identified through a combination of institutional outreach, community mobilisation and targeted referrals to ensure that eligible young people have fair access to the programme. First, Engee will work with the host institution’s entrepreneurship centre, career services, student affairs, academic departments and alumni networks to publicise the opportunity and identify potential participants. Faculty and staff will be encouraged to refer young people who show interest in entrepreneurship, digital and creative skills, employment or starting and growing a business. Second, we will use community networks and relevant youth-focused organisations to reach young people who may be outside formal institutional structures, including unemployed, out-of-school and underserved youth. Targeted outreach will be used to support the programme’s female and NEET participation targets. Interested applicants will complete a simple registration and screening process capturing relevant information such as age, employment or education status, interests, existing skills, business or career goals and availability. Selection will be based on transparent eligibility and programme-fit criteria. Selected beneficiaries will then be referred into the appropriate training, mentorship and enterprise-support activities based on their needs and interests. Participation and referral records will be maintained to track attendance, completion and progression. Regular follow-up will help identify beneficiaries who need additional mentorship, technical support, employment connections or enterprise referrals, ensuring that support continues beyond initial training.

inclusionAccessibilityCapacity: A+ Computer Training Technology Limited is committed to fostering an equitable, accessible, and inclusive learning ecosystem. Career Services & Placement Units: Facilitating internship pipelines, SIWES placements, CV clinics, and corporate recruiting events for graduating participants. Participants work on real-world industry briefs and capstone projects rather than hypothetical scenarios, ensuring skills directly address immediate employer talent gaps. Work Readiness & Career Prep Workshops: Alongside technical instruction, beneficiaries undergo intensive soft-skills conditioning, including technical interview prep, CV portfolio optimization, mock panel reviews, and professional workplace etiquette training. Direct Partner Matching & Talent Showcases: Upon project completion, we host structured Demo Days and Career Fairs connecting high-performing graduates directly with hiring managers. existingInstitutionalRelationships: Our relationship with host organizations is built on deep trust, mutual value, and long-term collaboration. institutionalCoordinationPlan: The work that we do at Mentor-Box is deeply anchored in existing public sector frameworks, most notably through our foundational partnership with the Kogi State Enterprise Development Agency (KEDA). staffFacultyEngagementPlan: To ensure programme success and sustainability, engaging institutional staff and faculty is critical to embedding our work into the very fabric of the academic environment rather than treating it as an outside intervention. beneficiaryReferralPlan: To ensure our programs reach the right people especially women and NEET youth who might otherwise slip through the cracks our beneficiary identification and referral process relies on a mix of grassroots community mobilization, institutional partnerships, and practical, aptitude-based screening. monitoringReportingSystems: Our data process begins right at recruitment, we use centralized digital collection tools like Google Forms to capture baseline data for each programme participant. employmentPathway: A key pillar of our employment pipeline is our collaboration with private-sector employers and development partners. governanceStructure: Labspace operates under a structured governance architecture designed to comply with the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA 2020) and address the operational peculiarities of running an innovation hub and ecosystem support organization (ESO) in Nigeria. The governance framework maintains a clear operational boundary between ownership, strategic oversight, and daily execution, ensuring that management operates strictly within delegated authority while key stakeholders retain necessary controls. The governance structure comprises four primary tiers: the Shareholders, who hold primary ownership rights and decide fundamental corporate transformations; the Board of Directors, which exercises strategic oversight, risk management, and fiduciary responsibilities; Executive Management, spearheaded by the CEO/Managing Director to drive daily execution; and specialized bodies such as Board Committees, an optional non-fiduciary Advisory Board for technical domains like AI and clean energy, and ecosystem entities. The Board of Directors functions as a cohesive fiduciary unit tasked with setting long-term strategy, ensuring regulatory compliance (including the Nigeria Startup Act 2022, tax regulations, and data protection laws), and monitoring financial sustainability. To maintain objective oversight, the framework incorporates Non-Executive Directors (NEDs) and Independent Non-Executive Directors (INEDs) appointed through a formal nomination process, subject to fixed three-year terms capped at a maximum of six to nine years, alongside mandatory retirement by rotation. Rigorous controls govern financial management, capital raising, and risk mitigation. Executive management must adhere to a Board-approved Delegation of Authority Matrix, maintain strict segregation of financial duties, enforce dual-authorization thresholds, and comply with Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering (SCUML) guidelines due to handling international donor grants and multi-currency transactions. Furthermore, strict policies govern conflict of interest, related-party transactions, and the protection of intellectual property. To protect foundational interests, the framework establishes a Reserved Matters Matrix. While standard corporate transformations require general shareholder approval, the framework grants specific veto and control protections to the Principal Founder (while holding at least 51% of ordinary shares) over anti-dilution, board and executive control, asset and IP protection, and material financial commitments. Unresolved deadlocks are subjected to executive negotiation, mediation, and binding arbitration in Lagos, ensuring stability and business continuity for the organisation.

governanceStructure: Corestream Networks and Robotics Limited (RC 1512578) operates a functional reporting structure built around a small executive management team, five operational department heads, and clearly defined lines of accountability from strategy down to service delivery. At the apex of the structure sits the Chief Executive Officer, Ibrahim Akorede Jimoh, who holds overall responsibility for corporate strategy, partnerships, investor relations, and product innovation. The CEO is supported by two C-suite executives and a Director of Learning, together forming the core executive management team that sets organisational direction and approves major decisions. The Chief Technology Officer, Walshak Timothy, leads all engineering, artificial intelligence, infrastructure, and architecture functions. Reporting into this office are five technical teams: Software Engineering, Mobile Development, AI & Research, DevOps & Infrastructure, and Quality Assurance. This structure allows Corestream to develop and maintain its core products — including CoreHealth and Wecare247 — while continuing applied research and platform-level infrastructure work in parallel. The Chief Operating Officer, Shamsudeen Abdulrazak, oversees Operations, spanning Finance, Human Resources, Procurement, Administration, and Compliance. This office ensures the organisation's internal controls, statutory compliance, and administrative systems are sound enough to support both commercial contracts and government-facing engagements. The Director of Learning, Sudais Abubakar, heads the Learning function, which delivers the company's training and capacity-building programmes — including 4E Africa and Coreskool — through a team of Training Coordinators and Facilitators. This division is central to Corestream's ability to execute large-scale, multi-state skills and education programmes. Two further functional areas complete the operational structure: a Business Development Lead, responsible for Sales, Partnerships, and Marketing, who drives client acquisition and strategic alliances; and a Digital Health Division, covering CoreHealth, Wecare247, Implementations, and Customer Success, which manages hospital deployments and ongoing client support. Governance follows a five-step accountability loop. First, Executive Management sets strategic direction. Second, department heads (the CTO, COO, Director of Learning, Business Development Lead, and Digital Health lead) translate that direction into operational plans for their respective functions. Third, team leads within each department supervise day-to-day project execution. Fourth, technical and support staff carry out the actual delivery of products and services. Fifth, and critically, performance data and outcomes flow back up through the same channels to Executive Management, which reviews results and adjusts strategy accordingly — closing the loop rather than leaving reporting as a one-way process. This structure currently supports a workforce of 38 — 4 in executive leadership, 16 in Technology, 6 in Digital Health, 7 in Learning, and 5 in Operations & Administration — of whom 31 are full-time employees and 7 are engaged on a project basis, allowing the organisation to flex capacity for time-bound programmes without disrupting its core team. Taken together, this governance model gives Corestream a structure that is deliberately compact at the top for fast decision-making, while functionally organised beneath it to run software development, digital health, AI, EdTech, government digital transformation, technical skills development, and innovation programmes simultaneously — with clear reporting lines and a built-in feedback mechanism for continuous improvement.

inclusionAccessibilityCapacity: Inclusion & Accessibility Capacity Corestream's inclusion strategy is built on a track record, not just a target: our current IDEAS Project TVET cohort already stands at 63% female participation, well above the 40% benchmark, demonstrating that our recruitment and delivery model organically attracts and retains women. governanceStructure: Codextel Limited operates through a structured governance and leadership framework designed to provide strategic oversight, operational accountability, financial stewardship, and effective management of its education, technology, creative, and digital development initiatives. The structure establishes clear lines of responsibility from executive leadership through technical and operational teams, enabling the organisation to efficiently manage both its internal operations and large-scale projects for public and private sector clients. At the apex of the organisation is the Board of Directors, which provides overall corporate governance and strategic oversight. The Board is responsible for guiding the long-term direction of Codextel, ensuring sound governance practices, monitoring organisational performance, and supporting executive management in major strategic and investment decisions. It also provides oversight on risk management, financial accountability, regulatory compliance, and the sustainability of the organisation. Reporting within this governance framework is the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), who provides overall strategic leadership for Codextel Limited. The CEO is responsible for translating the organisation's vision into actionable business and programme strategies, developing strategic partnerships, overseeing major client and stakeholder relationships, and ensuring that Codextel's activities remain aligned with its corporate objectives. The Chief Operating Officer (COO) provides leadership for the organisation's day-to-day operations and programme delivery. The COO coordinates operational teams, supports project planning and execution, and ensures effective collaboration across Codextel's technical and creative functions. This role provides the critical bridge between executive strategy and implementation. Financial governance is led by the Chief Financial Officer (CFO), who oversees financial planning, budgeting, expenditure management, financial controls, reporting, and resource allocation. The CFO supports management in maintaining financial discipline and ensuring that organisational and project resources are deployed responsibly. Codextel's executive leadership is supported by specialised team leads responsible for its core technical and creative functions. And for specialised assignments, Codextel’s core leadership structure is complemented by project experts in areas such as creative skills development, curriculum and training development, capacity building, research and policy analysis, gender and social inclusion, monitoring and evaluation, and field implementation.

inclusionAccessibilityCapacity: Codextel Limited will adopt a deliberate inclusive recruitment, participation and retention strategy to achieve and sustain the target of at least 40% female participation and 5% participation of NEET youth (Not in Education, Employment or Training). This approach builds on our experience delivering programmes for young people, in-school and out-of-school learners, teachers and underserved communities across Nigeria. To achieve the 40% female participation target, Codextel will establish gender targets from the beginning of beneficiary mobilisation rather than relying on general applications to produce the required representation. Recruitment data will be monitored throughout the application, screening and onboarding stages, with a minimum of 40% of available programme places reserved for qualified female participants. Outreach will specifically target women and girls through schools, tertiary institutions, community organisations, women-focused networks, creative communities and digital channels. Codextel will also address barriers that can prevent women from completing programmes. Training schedules and delivery formats will be designed to accommodate participants with family or caregiving responsibilities where practicable. Female mentors, trainers and creative-industry professionals will be incorporated into programme activities to provide visible role models and strengthen participants’ professional networks. Our Gender & Inclusion function will monitor participation, retention and completion rates and recommend corrective action where gender targets are at risk. For the minimum 5% NEET youth target, Codextel will undertake targeted mobilisation beyond conventional school and professional networks. Outreach will include community-based organisations, youth groups, local learning centres, grassroots networks and organisations working with unemployed and underserved young people. Our experience with out-of-school learners, community learning initiatives and adaptable digital learning formats provides a useful foundation for reaching participants who may not be connected to formal education or employment structures. Selection processes will recognise that NEET youth may have limited formal qualifications, portfolios or previous professional exposure. Where appropriate, Codextel will therefore use interest, aptitude, creativity and willingness to learn alongside conventional academic credentials when assessing candidates. Accessibility will also be integrated into programme delivery through simplified learning materials, visual and audio-based content, accessible digital resources and flexible learning approaches. Codextel’s existing experience developing story-based, visual and auditory learning content, including Hausa-language educational materials, demonstrates its capacity to adapt learning experiences to different literacy, language and accessibility needs. Finally, Codextel will maintain disaggregated beneficiary data covering gender, NEET status, location, enrolment, attendance, completion and outcomes. Progress against the 40% female and 5% NEET targets will be reviewed periodically, allowing recruitment or retention interventions to be adjusted early. This combination of targeted recruitment, reserved participation thresholds, accessible programme design, community outreach, inclusive selection and continuous monitoring will enable Codextel to move beyond nominal inclusion and achieve measurable participation and completion outcomes for women and underserved youth.
